chapter_theme: Short speeches of secret love and separation: the woman refusing the rains' sign or the town's sleep, dreams and wasted beauty, the friend's comforts and disclosures (the diviner's song, the tusker on his road), the lover's madal and his vow, and the strangers whose hearts mingle like rain in red earth (21-40).

21.reading: The woman says that even if the forest, where the new konrai flowers hang among their bee-thronged clusters like gold ornaments in women's hair, declares that the rains have come, she will not believe it, because he does not deal in lies.
21.nuance: She turns the season's sign against itself: if he has not come, this cannot be the rains he named, for he keeps his word. The forest is made to 'say' (கூறினும) like a witness she refuses, so her faith in him outweighs the evidence of the land.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest, the konrai and the word for the rainy season fix the mullai land and time

comparisons.tenor: the golden konrai clusters showing in the forest

22.reading: The friend tells the weeping woman that no one would part from her and leave her here with streaming eyes: his journey will be made with her, she whose bright brow is fragrant as the spring branches of the whorled maraa that adorns the hill slope.
22.nuance: 'நின்னொடுஞ் செலவே' can mean that he will take her with him or that he cannot go at all without her; either way the friend answers the fear of parting by denying that it can happen.

thinai_evidence.note: the fear of his leaving on a journey is the paalai situation

comparisons.tenor: her brow, fragrant as the maraa's spring branches

23.reading: The friend calls on the diviner woman, whose long fine hair is like a strung row of shell beads, to sing her song, and sing it again: the song she sang of his tall good hill.
23.nuance: By asking for the song about his hill, the friend lets the rite itself disclose whom the girl pines for, without naming him before the household. The triple call அகவன் மகளே and the triple பாட்டே copy the chant of the rite.

thinai_evidence.note: his tall hill is the land of the love and of the song

24.reading: The woman asks whether the new bounty of the dark-trunked neem's bright flowers will pass without her, and says that since her lover went away the tongues of the cruel have clamoured until she is crushed like a single fig fruit trodden by an elephant beside the river.
24.nuance: The neem's flowering marks a season meant to be shared; the gossip, not the absence alone, is what crushes her, and one fallen fruit under a great beast measures how small she is against the town's tongues.

thinai_evidence.note: she endures the season through while he is away

comparisons.tenor: she, crushed by the gossip that rose when he left

25.reading: The woman says that no one was there but the thief himself, and if he goes back on his word she can do nothing; only a heron was there, on thin green legs like millet stalks, watching the running water for aaral fish, on the day he took her.
25.nuance: The one witness of the union is a heron whose eyes were on the fish, a witness that saw nothing; கள்வன் names the secret lover as a thief who left no proof.

thinai_evidence.note: the secret union with no witness is the kalavu of kurinji

26.reading: The friend says that though the man of the land where peacocks perched on the high branches of the fully bloomed dark-trunked vengai look like women plucking flowers should speak falsely, like one unworthy, what one has seen with one's own eyes does not lie; even the male monkey of the hill, sire of a sturdy young one, sharp-toothed and red-mouthed, eating sweet mango, knows that cruel man.
26.nuance: Against the lover's possible denial the friend calls the hill's own creature as witness. Who 'தான்' and 'தன்கண்' refer to is not fixed (the lover, or a diviner who speaks wrongly of the girl's illness), so the occasion is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai, the hill and its monkey fix the land

comparisons.tenor: the peacocks perched on the vengai's high branches
the lover, if he speaks falsely

27.reading: The woman says that her beauty, the dark glow of her mottled waist, of use neither to herself nor to her man, is left for pallor to eat, like a good cow's sweet milk that the calf does not drink and the pail does not catch, spilling on the ground.
27.nuance: The simile makes beauty a yield owed to someone; unshared, it is not only lost but wasted, and உணீஇயர் gives the pallor an eater's appetite.

thinai_evidence.note: beauty wasting into pallor while her man is away

comparisons.tenor: her beauty, enjoyed by no one and eaten by pallor

28.reading: The woman asks whether she should butt them, or strike them, or, not knowing what to do, find some pretext and cry out 'aah, help' to the town that sleeps on, unaware of the grief that torments her while the restless wind tosses her about.
28.nuance: Her rage is at the sleeping town, not at the man: the whole community rests while she alone keeps watch with her pain, and the wind is the only thing awake with her.

thinai_evidence.note: the grief of a woman left alone

29.reading: The man tells his heart that, passing over good counsel and spreading worthless talk, it has plunged like a fresh unfired pot set out in the rain into a flood the mind cannot hold, and is in hard straits; its clamour would be very great indeed, if it found anyone to hold it close and listen, as a mother monkey on a high branch holds her young.
29.nuance: The unfired pot dissolves in the very water it takes in: the heart is unmade by the desire it receives. The second simile is a wish that sharpens the loneliness: no one will hold and hear him as the monkey holds her child.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey on the high branch is of the hill

comparisons.tenor: the heart that took in a flood of desire it cannot hold
one who would hold the heart close and listen

30.reading: The woman tells her friend to listen: last night a lying dream that seemed true, of the embrace of the man so skilled in lies, deceived her, and she rose and felt over the bed; now, wasted like a kuvalai flower that the bees have visited, she is alone and truly to be pitied.
30.nuance: The man is called a master of lies and the dream a lie that looked true, so the dream repeats his falseness; waking is the moment of loss, her hand finding the empty bed.

thinai_evidence.note: she wakes alone in his absence

comparisons.tenor: she, wasted and alone after the dream

31.reading: The woman says that neither at the festival where warriors gather nor in the thunangai dance where women hold one another can she find the noble one anywhere; she too is a woman of the dancing ground, and the proud chief who loosened her bright conch bangles is a man of the dancing ground as well.
31.nuance: The poet is Aathimanthiyaar, and the lost man of the dancing ground is the dancer whom other poems name; she searches the festival grounds because they are his own place, and the two parallel lines (ஆடுகள மகளே, ஆடுகள மகனே) claim an equal bond.

thinai_evidence.note: the town's festival and its dance are marutham settings

32.reading: The man says that if one can tell the hours apart, morning, day, helpless evening, the midnight when the town sleeps, and dawn, then love is a lie; to appear in the street on the palmyra-stem horse and proclaim it openly is shame, and to go on living is shame too, once parting comes.
32.nuance: The two shames are made equal: riding the madal disgraces him, but living apart from her is no less a disgrace, so the threat is the lesser of two dishonours. Tholkappiyam files madal under perunthinai; here it is threatened, not yet done, and the poem stays in kurinji.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover in secret love threatens madal to win her

comparisons.tenor: the palmyra stem ridden as a horse

33.reading: The woman says to her companion that this young student, his body never filled by the food he begs, who comes into town as a guest, such a great noble fellow, must be someone of standing at the common ground of his own town.
33.nuance: The praise is mockery: the go-between who comes begging as a guest is called a great man, so the heroine shuts him out with laughter instead of anger. Whose messenger he is, and whether அன்னாய் addresses the friend or the mother, the poem does not say.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names no land; the colophon's marutham and the refusal of a go-between are followed

34.reading: The friend says: let this town, which would not stop when we rebuked it nor believe when we denied, now that its gossip that we sleep alone is over, hear the sweet news and rejoice: the lord of our girl, whose bright brow with its shining ear-rings is lovely as Kuttuvan's Maranthai, where the great flock of herons in the seaside grove takes fright at the roar of the warriors, is that very man.
34.nuance: The gossip ends by coming true: the man the town whispered about is now her lord (கிழவனும் அவனே), so the friend invites the town to the very news it guessed. The brow is measured by the beauty of a Chera port town.

thinai_evidence.note: the gossip of the town ends when the man is owned as her lord

comparisons.tenor: the girl's bright brow and beauty

35.reading: The woman says her eyes are shameless indeed; and the cold north wind, coming with fine drizzle that opens the folded bud of the dense sugarcane, swollen like the belly of a green snake heavy with young on a branch, is fire to those who have been parted.
35.nuance: The cane's flower opening in the drizzle is a sign of fruitfulness that burns the parted woman; her shameless eyes weep openly and betray her.

thinai_evidence.note: the pain of the one parted from her man

comparisons.tenor: the folded flower-bud of the sugarcane

36.reading: The woman tells her friend that the man of the hill land, where the dark maanai creeper climbs an elephant asleep beside a boulder, swore an unfailing vow, 'with my heart as witness I will not leave you', on the day he took her shoulders; is the grief then yours, friend?
36.nuance: The creeper that climbs the sleeping elephant as though it were the boulder beside it is a near miss for ullurai: one correspondence (a clinging thing on a body unaware of it) but no second pair, so it stays scene. His vow is called வஞ்சினம், the warrior's word.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill, its boulder, creeper and elephant

37.reading: The friend tells the woman that he has great desire for her and will surely be gracious; the road he took is a loving one, where the big-trunked tusker strips the soft branches of the yaa tree to ease the hunger of his mate.
37.nuance: The friend calls the road itself 'loving' (அன்பின) because of what is done on it: the hero cannot pass such care without being reminded of his own.

thinai_evidence.note: the yaa tree and the hungry elephants of the dry road

iraicchi.act: the tusker strips the yaa tree's soft branches to ease his mate's hunger
iraicchi.sense: the man who sees such care on his road will remember his own wife and return to cherish her

38.reading: The woman says, bitterly, that the friendship of the hill man, in whose land the young of the sun-basking langur roll the eggs the forest peahen laid on a rock, is good indeed for ever, friend, for those who can bear it without thinking of him while their kohl-lined eyes are spent with tears.
38.nuance: The praise is irony: his bond is good only for one who can forget him. The langur's young rolling the peahen's eggs on bare rock is a near miss for ullurai (one correspondence, careless play with a fragile thing left exposed, but no second pair), so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the peahen, the langur and the hill

39.reading: The woman says they tell her that the road taken by him who tired of lying between her breasts is the hard mountain waste where, when the fierce strong wind sweeps through the grove, the dried ripe pods of the uzhinjil rattle.
39.nuance: 'என்ப', they say: she knows the road only by report, and the rattling pods are the sound she imagines on it. முனிநர், the one who tired of her, makes his leaving a rejection, not only a journey.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard dry waste with its rattling dead pods

40.reading: The man asks what his mother and hers were to each other, how his father and hers are kin, and how he and she ever came to know each other; yet like rain falling on red earth, their loving hearts have mingled into one.
40.nuance: The three questions strip away every tie of kin and acquaintance before the simile, so the union owes nothing to family; rain on red soil takes its colour and cannot be separated out again. The poet is known only by this image (செம்புலப் பெயனீரார்).

thinai_evidence.note: the first union of two strangers in secret love

comparisons.tenor: two loving hearts mingled into one

links.note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend points to the bloomed konrai that has made the forest lovely as proof that the season of his return has come. Kuruntokai 21: the woman says that even if the konrai forest declares the rains, she will not believe it, since he does not lie.
links.teaches: The same konrai sign is proof of his return in the friend's mouth and a sign the woman refuses in her own, so the season argument of the mullai poems could be turned around: faith in his word can deny the season rather than read it.

links.note: Kuruntokai 25: the only witness of the secret union was a heron watching for fish. Kuruntokai 26: against the lover's possible denial, the friend says even the male monkey of the hill knows that cruel man.
links.teaches: Held together, the two poems show the lack of a human witness to kalavu as a standing fear, answered by pointing to the land's own creatures: the woman doubts that the heron saw anything, while the friend insists that the monkey knows.

links.note: Kural 1189: the woman says let her body turn pale as it will, if the man who persuaded her is well. Kuruntokai 27: her beauty, of use neither to her nor to him, is left for pallor to eat, like milk spilt on the ground.
links.teaches: The Kural lets the woman accept pallor as a price paid for his welfare, while the Kuruntokai poet counts it pure waste, a yield that reaches no one, so the same pallor in absence is read as sacrifice in one and as loss with no gain in the other.

links.note: Kural 1168: the night, which puts all living beings to sleep, is to be pitied, for it has no companion but her. Kuruntokai 28: she wants to strike, butt or cry out at the town that sleeps unaware of her pain.
links.teaches: Both set one sleepless woman against a sleeping world, but the Kural turns the loneliness into pity for the night, while the Sangam poem turns it into rage at the town, which shows that the same isolation could be voiced as tender complaint or as a wish to wake everyone.

links.note: Kural 1229: when evening spreads, the whole town is bewildered and suffers (on the reading that the town shares her pain). Kuruntokai 28: the town sleeps, not knowing her grief.
links.teaches: On that reading the Kural imagines the town grieving with the lovesick woman, while Kuruntokai 28 has the town sleep through her grief, so whether the community shares a private sorrow is answered both ways in the love poetry.

links.note: Kural 660: making wealth by deceit and feeling safe is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. Kuruntokai 29: the heart, passing over good counsel, is like a fresh unfired pot set out in the rain, plunged into a flood it cannot hold.
links.teaches: In both the unfired pot is ruined by what it is made to hold, so the image locates the fault in the vessel rather than the water: wealth got by fraud undoes its keeper as desire taken in against counsel undoes the heart.

links.note: Kural 1216: if there were no waking, the lover in the dream would not leave. Kuruntokai 30: a lying dream of his embrace deceived her, and she rose and felt over the bed, alone.
links.teaches: The Kural blames waking in the abstract, while the Kuruntokai poem shows the very moment, the hand on the empty bed, so the couplet's complaint gains a scene and the scene gains a name for its cause.

links.note: Kural 1218: in sleep he is on her shoulder, and when she wakes he quickly moves into her heart. Kuruntokai 30: on waking from the dream she finds only the empty bed and calls herself alone and pitiable.
links.teaches: The Kural consoles the dreamer that waking only moves the lover inward, while the Kuruntokai woman finds no such refuge and is left alone, so the two disagree on whether the waking after a love dream is a loss or a passage into the heart.

links.note: Akananuru 236 likens the heroine to Aathimanthi, who wept from land to land and town to town asking 'have you not seen Aattan Atthi?', the dancer the flood took. Kuruntokai 31, by Aathimanthiyaar, has a woman of the dancing ground search festival and dance for the chief who is a man of the dancing ground.
links.teaches: Read with Paranar's simile, the unnamed 'man of the dancing ground' in Kuruntokai 31 is the lost dancer of the legend, and the poem gives in the first person the search the Akananuru turns into a stock comparison for a woman maddened by loss.

links.note: Akananuru 222 tells how Aathimanthi, after the Kaveri seized Aattan Atthi, searched in bewilderment until Maruthi showed her the lover and entered the sea. Kuruntokai 31 is the woman's own voice at the stage where she finds him nowhere.
links.teaches: Together the two poems order the story: Kuruntokai 31 stands in the middle of the search, 'nowhere do I see him', and the Akananuru supplies the end that the short poem never reaches, so the legend outlived the poet's own lament.

links.note: Kural 1131: for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and no strength but the palmyra horse. Kuruntokai 32: to ride the madal in the street is shame, and to live apart is shame too.
links.teaches: The same lover's threat is a safeguard in the Kural and a disgrace in the Kuruntokai, which only weighs it as the lesser of two shames, so the madal was argued both as the lover's last strength and as an equal dishonour to living on without her.

links.note: Kural 1227: love-sickness buds in the morning, ripens through the day and opens in the evening. Kuruntokai 32: if one can tell morning, day, evening, midnight and dawn apart, love is a lie.
links.teaches: The Kural gives love a daily clock with evening as its worst hour, while the Kuruntokai lover says true love cannot tell the hours apart, so the two set the convention of the evening's pain against the claim that real longing knows no time.

links.note: Akananuru 376: the courtesan asks the lord to give back her beauty, which was like Kuttuvan's Maranthai. Kuruntokai 34: the friend calls the wife's bright brow lovely as Kuttuvan's Maranthai.
links.teaches: The same Chera port is the standard of beauty for a wedded girl and for a courtesan, so the akam poets used Maranthai's fame as a neutral measure of a woman's nalam whatever her standing.

links.note: Purananuru 71: Boothappandiyan vows that if he does not rout the allied kings he may be parted from his wide-eyed wife. Kuruntokai 36: the lover swore a vanjinam that he would not leave her.
links.teaches: Separation from the beloved is the penalty the king stakes on his battle vow and the very thing the lover's vow forswears, so the akam vow borrows the puram form and the friend's trust in it rests on the warrior's honour that a vanjinam is never broken.

links.note: Akananuru 59: the friend tells the wasting heroine that on the road the man took a tusker bends a tall yaa tree to feed its young mate, and the poem ends on 'the road he went'. Kuruntokai 37 gives the same tusker easing its mate's hunger on the yaa and the same close, 'the road he went'.
links.teaches: The long poem spends its lines on her lost beauty, a Mal simile and his forgetting before reaching the tusker and the road, so Kuruntokai 37 shows the consolation reduced to its working parts: a promise of his love, the creature's care as proof, and the road.

links.note: Kalittokai 11: the woman says the man himself told her that in the burning forest the tusker lets his mate drink the little muddy water first, the dove fans its tired mate and the stag shades the doe, so he will return. Kuruntokai 37: the friend gives one tusker stripping the yaa for his mate.
links.teaches: The later Kalittokai multiplies the single tusker into three caring males and puts the inference in the heroine's own mouth, which shows the comforting iraicchi of porul 5.35 growing from the friend's one proof into a catalogue the heroine argues from.

links.note: Akananuru 45: the lover crossed a summer forest where the dried pods of the uzhunjil rattle like the drums of a dancing ground. Kuruntokai 39: they say his road is the hard waste where the wind makes the dried uzhinjil pods rattle.
links.teaches: The rattling uzhinjil pods are a fixed sign by which a waiting woman pictures the man's road; the Akananuru makes the sound a dance drum, while Kuruntokai 39 keeps it as hearsay ('they say'), showing that the woman's knowledge of the waste is report, not sight.

links.note: Kural 1122: the man says the bond between him and the girl is that of body and life. Kuruntokai 40: the man says their mothers, fathers and they themselves were strangers, yet their loving hearts have mingled like rain in red earth.
links.teaches: Both men declare an inseparable bond, but the Kuruntokai first denies any tie of kin, so the union it praises is made between strangers and inseparable only after mingling, which the Kural's body-and-life image, a pair joined from birth, does not show.

new_concepts.gloss: the woman diviner who sings of the hills to find the cause of a girl's illness, through whose song the friend may disclose the secret love

source_issues: 29: the colophon thurai reads தலைன் கூற்று; தலைவன் கூற்று is meant (the speaker addresses his own heart).
24 line 4: குளிறு is read as களிறு, elephant (எழுகளிறு); the construction of lines 3 to 6 is uncertain and the verse is marked uncertain.
34 line 4: முனாஅது யானையங் குருகின் is obscure (the bird யானையங் குருகு and the sense of முனாஅது); the Maranthai simile is read without fixing it, and the verse is marked uncertain.
33: the poem does not say whose go-between the young student is, nor whether அன்னாய் addresses the friend or the mother; marked uncertain.
